claim: Metagenomics and single-cell genomics have enabled genome discovery from unknown branches of life.
source: Metagenomics and single-cell genomics have enabled genome discovery from unknown branches of life.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of metagenomics and single-cell genomics, presented as established fact in the abstract.

claim: Extracting novel genomes from complex mixtures of metagenomic data can be challenging and represents an ill-posed problem which is generally approached with ad hoc methods.
source: However, extracting novel genomes from complex mixtures of metagenomic data can still be challenging and represents an ill-posed problem which is generally approached with ad hoc methods.
evidence: This statement describes current limitations in the field, presented as established knowledge about metagenomic analysis challenges.

claim: The microfluidic-based mini-metagenomic method offers a statistically rigorous approach to extract novel microbial genomes while preserving single-cell resolution.
source: Here we present a microfluidic-based mini-metagenomic method which offers a statistically rigorous approach to extract novel microbial genomes while preserving single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the method presented in the manuscript, supported by the experimental data and analyses described throughout the paper.

claim: The mini-metagenomic approach was used to analyze two hot spring samples from Yellowstone National Park and extracted 29 new genomes, including three deeply branching lineages.
source: We used this approach to analyze two hot spring samples from Yellowstone National Park and extracted 29 new genomes, including three deeply branching lineages.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including genome assembly and phylogenetic analysis results.

claim: The single-cell resolution enabled accurate quantification of genome function and abundance, down to 1% in relative abundance.
source: The single-cell resolution enabled accurate quantification of genome function and abundance, down to 1% in relative abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the abundance quantification data presented in Figure 6 and related analyses.

claim: Analyses of genome level SNP distributions revealed low to moderate environmental selection.
source: Our analyses of genome level SNP distributions also revealed low to moderate environmental selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by SNP analysis data and dN/dS ratio calculations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The total number of sequenced microbial genomes is more than 50,000 as of December 1, 2016.
source: These studies revealed many previously uncharacterized genomes (Brown et al., 2015; Eloe-Fadrosh et al., 2016; Kashtan et al., 2014; Rinke et al., 2013), increasing the total number of sequenced microbial genomes to more than 50,000 (Joint Genome Institute's Integrated Microbial Genomes database, accessed December 1, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Joint Genome Institute's Integrated Microbial Genomes database.

claim: The majority of environmental microbial diversity remains uncharacterized due to limitations in current techniques.
source: However, the majority of environmental microbial diversity remains uncharacterized due to limitations in current techniques.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the state of microbial diversity characterization.

claim: Conventional shotgun metagenomic sequencing is effective only if the complexity of the sample is not too great.
source: Conventional shotgun metagenomic sequencing offers the ability to assemble genomes from a single heterogeneous sample, but is effective only if the complexity of the sample is not too great (Howe et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Howe et al., 2014.

claim: It is often difficult to separate contigs belonging to closely related organisms because techniques designed to resolve these differences, such as tetranucleotide analysis, depend on ad hoc assumptions about nucleotide usage.
source: Furthermore, it is often difficult to separate contigs belonging to closely related organisms because techniques designed to resolve these differences, such as tetranucleotide analysis, depend on ad hoc assumptions about nucleotide usage (Dick et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dick et al., 2009.

claim: Single-cell sequencing approaches performed in plates are typically expensive and laborious.
source: In addition, when performed in plates, single-cell sequencing approaches are typically expensive and laborious, although microfluidic approaches have helped to alleviate that limitation (Blainey et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blainey et al., 2011 and represents established knowledge about single-cell sequencing methods.

claim: The mini-metagenomics approach uses microfluidic parallelization to separate an environmental sample into many small sub-samples containing 5–10 cells.
source: This approach uses microfluidic parallelization to separate an environmental sample into many small sub-samples containing 5–10 cells, significantly reducing complexity of each sub-sample and allowing high quality assembly while enabling higher throughput than typical single-cell methods.
evidence: This is a description of the method supported by the experimental design and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Single-cell resolution is regained through correlations of genome co-occurrence across sub-samples.
source: Although each sub-sample contains a limited mixture of several genomes, single-cell resolution is regained through correlations of genome co-occurrence across sub-samples, which in turn enables a rigorous statistical interpretation of confidence and genome association.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bioinformatic analysis methods and results presented in the manuscript, particularly the co-occurrence analysis.

claim: Among 29 genomes larger than 0.5 Mbps, most belong to known bacterial and archaeal phyla but represent novel lineages at lower taxonomic levels.
source: Among 29 genomes larger than 0.5 Mbps, most belong to known bacterial and archaeal phyla but represent novel lineages at lower taxonomic levels; three genomes represent deeply branching novel phylogenies.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data presented in Figure 4 and related analyses.

claim: Three genomes represent deeply branching novel phylogenies.
source: Among 29 genomes larger than 0.5 Mbps, most belong to known bacterial and archaeal phyla but represent novel lineages at lower taxonomic levels; three genomes represent deeply branching novel phylogenies.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Functional analysis revealed different metabolic pathways that cells may use to achieve the same biochemical process such as nitrogen and sulfur reduction.
source: Functional analysis revealed different metabolic pathways that cells may use to achieve the same biochemical process such as nitrogen and sulfur reduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional analysis data presented in Figure 5.

claim: 96 lysis and MDA reactions are performed in independent chambers of an automated and commercially available Fluidigm C1 Integrated Fluidic Circuit.
source: 96 lysis and MDA (Multiple Displacement Amplification) reactions are performed in independent chambers of an automated and commercially available Fluidigm C1 Integrated Fluidic Circuit (IFC) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which significantly reduces the time and effort required to perform these reactions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method supported by Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C1 IFC has been used previously for mammalian single-cell RNA-seq and genome analysis experiments.
source: The C1 IFC has been used previously for mammalian single-cell RNA-seq and genome analysis experiments (Wu et al., 2014; Pollen et al., 2014; Treutlein et al., 2014; Gawad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The hardware, including the microfluidic circuit, was not altered for the mini-metagenomic experiments.
source: The hardware, including the microfluidic circuit, was not altered for the mini-metagenomic experiments, but we did adapt a new reagent kit and designed scripts and protocols for amplifying genomic DNA from microbial cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Smaller MDA reaction volumes (~300 nL) are associated with lower gain and less amplification bias, which effectively improves coverage uniformity of amplified genomes.
source: In addition, smaller MDA reaction volumes (~300 nL) are associated with lower gain and less amplification bias, which effectively improves coverage uniformity of amplified genomes (de Bourcy et al., 2014) (Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Bourcy et al., 2014.

claim: The enclosed reaction environment of the microfluidic platform limits potential contamination often observed with low input MDA reactions in well plates.
source: Another advantage of using a microfluidic platform is the enclosed reaction environment that limits potential contamination often observed with low input MDA reactions in well plates, a problem that, with other approaches, requires sophisticated protocols for contamination prevention and removal (Woyke et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Woyke et al., 2011 and represents an advantage of the method.

claim: Thirty mini-metagenomic and 36 single-cell limiting dilution sub-samples yielded 169 and 194 million paired end reads, respectively.
source: Thirty mini-metagenomic and 36 single-cell limiting dilution sub-samples yielded 169 and 194 million paired end reads, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of sequencing data from the mock community experiment.

claim: Initial trimming removed 14 ± 1.1% (s.d.) reads.
source: Initial trimming removed 14 ± 1.1% (s.d.) reads; 80 ± 1.5% (s.d.) of the remaining reads mapped uniquely to reference genomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 80 ± 1.5% (s.d.) of the remaining reads mapped uniquely to reference genomes.
source: Initial trimming removed 14 ± 1.1% (s.d.) reads; 80 ± 1.5% (s.d.) of the remaining reads mapped uniquely to reference genomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Unmapped reads made up only 3% of all reads.
source: Unmapped reads made up only 3% of all reads (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Chimeras represented <1% of the reads.
source: Improperly mapped reads (3 ± 0.9% s.d.) were mostly short, low quality sequences, and chimeras represented <1% of the reads.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the mock community analysis.

claim: Mini-metagenomic MDA reactions produced higher median coverage than single-cell MDA reactions at all sequencing depths.
source: Mini-metagenomic MDA reactions produced higher median coverage than single-cell MDA reactions at all sequencing depths (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The proportion of assembled genome as a function of aligned genome did not differ significantly between mini-metagenomic and single-cell methods.
source: The proportion of assembled genome as a function of aligned genome, however, did not differ significantly between mini-metagenomic and single-cell methods (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: With the mini-metagenomic method, less sequencing cost is required to recover similar genome coverage as compared to single-cell experiments, with the improvement mostly associated with the amplification rather than assembly steps.
source: Therefore, data from mock bacterial communities demonstrate that with the mini-metagenomic method, less sequencing cost is required to recover similar genome coverage as compared to single-cell experiments, with the improvement mostly associated with the amplification rather than assembly steps.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis of mini-metagenomic and single-cell methods using the mock community.

claim: Sample #1 was collected from Bijah Spring and sample #2 was collected from Mound Spring.
source: Sample #1 was collected from Bijah Spring and sample #2 was collected from Mound Spring (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about sample collection supported by Table 2.

claim: 121 and 133 million paired end reads were obtained from the two samples respectively.
source: 121 and 133 million paired end reads were obtained from the two samples respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of sequencing data.

claim: After quality filtering, >90% reads from each sub-sample were incorporated into contigs during independent assemblies.
source: After quality filtering, >90% reads from each sub-sample were incorporated into contigs during independent assemblies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Re-assembling combined sub-sample reads increased contig length.
source: Re-assembling combined sub-sample reads increased contig length (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 643 and 1474 contigs longer than 10 kbp were obtained from the two samples, respectively.
source: We obtained 643 and 1474 contigs longer than 10 kbp from the two samples, respectively, and used these contigs for subsequent analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and Table 3.

claim: For the Bijah Spring sample, where 49 sub-samples were available, the shotgun metagenomic assembly produced more contigs over 10 kbp.
source: After assembly (Materials and methods), we observed that for the Bijah Spring sample, where 49 sub-samples were available, the shotgun metagenomic assembly produced more contigs over 10 kbp (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: For the Mound Spring sample, where 93 sub-samples were used, the mini-metagenomic assembly produced more contigs over 10 kbp.
source: However, for the Mound Spring sample, where 93 sub-samples were used, the mini-metagenomic assembly produced more contigs over 10 kbp.
evidence: This is a direct report of assembly comparison results.

claim: The largest contig from the mini-metagenomic assembly was longer for the Mound Spring sample.
source: The largest contig from the mini-metagenomic assembly was also longer for the Mound Spring sample (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Increasing the number of mini-metagenomic sub-samples likely improves assembly performance compared to shotgun metagenomics.
source: Therefore, it is likely that increasing the number of mini-metagenomic sub-samples improves assembly performance compared to shotgun metagenomics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of assembly results between Bijah and Mound Spring samples.

claim: The observed assembly improvement may be due to higher complexity of the Mound Spring bacterial community.
source: It is also possible that the observed assembly improvement is due to higher complexity of the Mound Spring bacterial community, validating our hypothesis that the mini-metagenomic method benefits the analysis of complex microbial populations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the assembly comparison results.

claim: Approximately 70% of all contigs were assigned at the phylum level.
source: Approximately 70% of all contigs were assigned at the phylum level.
evidence: This is a direct report of annotation results.

claim: Contigs with known assignment and from the same cluster always belonged to the same phylum.
source: Contigs with known assignment and from the same cluster always belonged to the same phylum, demonstrating that the presence-based method can correctly bin metagenomic contigs into genomes (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the contig clustering and annotation results presented in Figure 2C,D.

claim: 29 partial genome bins from both hot spring samples with genome sizes over 0.5 Mbp were selected for downstream analyses.
source: We selected 29 partial genome bins from both hot spring samples with genome sizes over 0.5 Mbp for downstream analyses (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the selection criteria for genome bins.

claim: Assessment of genome bins demonstrated various levels of completeness and <5% marker gene duplication.
source: Assessment of genome bins demonstrated various levels of completeness and <5% marker gene duplication (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Eight genome bins with known phylum level assignments were identified from the Bijah Spring sample.
source: Using lineage assignment based on gene annotations, we identified eight genome bins with known phylum level assignments from the Bijah Spring sample.
evidence: This is a direct report of phylogenetic assignment results.

claim: Three genomes (Bijah #3, Bijah #5, and Bijah #14) had unknown assignments.
source: Three genomes (Bijah #3, Bijah #5, and Bijah #14) had unknown assignments (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic assignment results presented in Figure 2C.

claim: In the Mound Spring sample, 14 genomes with known phylum level assignments and three unassigned genomes (Mound #3, Mound #4, and Mound #7) were extracted.
source: In the Mound Spring sample, more reads and sub-samples resulted in 14 genomes with known phylum level assignments and three unassigned genomes (Mound #3, Mound #4, and Mound #7) were extracted (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic assignment results presented in Figure 2D.

claim: A singleton contig 3.3 Mbp in length (#40) was included as a separate genome.
source: A singleton contig 3.3 Mbp in length (#40) was also included as a separate genome.
evidence: This is a direct statement about genome identification.

claim: The ability to separate distinct clusters of Bacteroidetes contigs represents an advantage of the sequence-independent binning approach.
source: In both environmental samples, the ability to separate distinct clusters of Bacteroidetes contigs represents an advantage of our sequence-independent binning approach, where the presence of bacterial species across microfluidic chambers is determined only by Poisson distribution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the binning results, supported by the data showing distinct Bacteroidetes clusters.

claim: Seventeen genomes, including four unassigned genomes, were complete enough for phylogenetic tree construction based on 56 single copy marker genes.
source: Seventeen genomes (shown in bold in Figure 2C,D), including four unassigned genomes, were complete enough for phylogenetic tree construction based on 56 single copy marker genes (Eloe-Fadrosh et al., 2016) (Figure 4; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: All marker gene based phylogenetic assignments were consistent with annotation based assignments.
source: All marker gene based phylogenetic assignments were consistent with annotation based assignments.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the consistency of phylogenetic assignment methods.

claim: 13 genomes with short to medium branch length from known lineages were identified.
source: We identified 13 genomes with short to medium branch length from known lineages (red), and four deeply branching lineages that may represent potentially novel phyla (red and starred).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree presented in Figure 4.

claim: Four deeply branching lineages that may represent potentially novel phyla were identified.
source: We identified 13 genomes with short to medium branch length from known lineages (red), and four deeply branching lineages that may represent potentially novel phyla (red and starred).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree presented in Figure 4.

claim: Partial archaeal genomes belonging to Euryarchaeota (Mound #16) and Bathyarchaeota (Mound #14) were extracted.
source: In addition to bacterial lineages, we also extracted partial archaeal genomes belonging to Euryarchaeota (Mound #16) and Bathyarchaeota (Mound #14) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Phylogenetic trees built from blast results of individual ribosomal protein sequences suggest that both genomes Bijah #14 and Mound #3 belonged to the phylum Ignavibacteriae.
source: Phylogenetic trees built from blast results of individual ribosomal protein sequences suggest that both genomes belonged to the phylum Ignavibacteriae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Mound Spring population displayed higher potential for methanogenesis than the Bijah Spring population.
source: At the community level, the Mound Spring population displayed higher potential for methanogenesis than the Bijah Spring population, and methanogenesis can be carried out by members of the Euryarchaeota (Mound # 16) lineages involving mcr and hdr complex (Ferry, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data presented in Figure 5 and citation to Ferry, 2011.

claim: Methanogenesis can be carried out by members of the Euryarchaeota (Mound # 16) lineages involving mcr and hdr complex.
source: At the community level, the Mound Spring population displayed higher potential for methanogenesis than the Bijah Spring population, and methanogenesis can be carried out by members of the Euryarchaeota (Mound # 16) lineages involving mcr and hdr complex (Ferry, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data and citation to Ferry, 2011.

claim: Formaldehyde assimilation could be carried out in both communities.
source: Formaldehyde assimilation, on the other hand, could be carried out in both communities.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Five genomes including Ignavibacteriae (Mound #40), Bacteroidetes (Mound #2), Nitrospirae (Mound #19), Thermodesulfobacteria (Mound #21), and Ignavibacteriae (Bijah #2) carry nar, nrf, and nir genes, possibly participating in the conversion of nitrate to ammonia.
source: In nitrogen metabolism, we identified five genomes including Ignavibacteriae (Mound #40), Bacteroidetes (Mound #2), Nitrospirae (Mound #19), Thermodesulfobacteria (Mound #21), and Ignavibacteriae (Bijah #2) carrying nar, nrf, and nir genes, possibly participating in the conversion of nitrate to ammonia (Sodergren and DeMoss, 1988; Einsle et al., 1999; Cantera and Stein, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data and citations to Sodergren and DeMoss, 1988; Einsle et al., 1999; Cantera and Stein, 2007.

claim: The archaeal genome belonging to Bathyarchaeota (Mound #14) carries nifD and nifH, capable of converting nitrogen directly to ammonia.
source: Interestingly, the archaeal genome belonging to Bathyarchaeota (Mound #14) carries nifD and nifH, capable of converting nitrogen directly to ammonia (Fani et al., 2000) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data presented in Figure 5B and citation to Fani et al., 2000.

claim: A genome extracted from Bijah Spring belonging to Spirochaetes carried nirS, norBC, and nosZ genes, capable of reducing nitrite to nitrogen.
source: Although we did not identify denitrification genes in the Mound Spring community, a genome extracted from Bijah Spring belonging to Spirochaetes carried nirS, norBC, and nosZ genes, capable of reducing nitrite to nitrogen (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Bacterial clades associated with thermophilic environments in the Yellowstone National Park are known for their sulfur reduction activities.
source: Bacterial clades associated with thermophilic environments in the Yellowstone National Park are known for their sulfur reduction (converting sulfate to sulfide) activities (Henry et al., 1994; Inskeep et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henry et al., 1994 and Inskeep et al., 2013.

claim: Genes associated with the assimilatory sulfate reduction pathway (cysNC, sat, cysC, cysH, and cysI) were identified from three Mound Spring genomes including Ignavibacteriae (Mound #40), Bacteroidetes (Mound #2), Fervidibacteria (Mound #8) and one Bijah Spring genome – Spirochaetes (Bijah #7).
source: We identified genes associated with the assimilatory sulfate reduction pathway (cysNC, sat, cysC, cysH, and cysI) from three Mound Spring genomes including Ignavibacteriae (Mound #40), Bacteroidetes (Mound #2), Fervidibacteria (Mound #8) and one Bijah Spring genome – Spirochaetes (Bijah #7).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data.

claim: Key genes (dsrAB) responsible for dissimilatory sulfate reduction were identified from Nitrospirae (Mound #19) and Termodesulfobacteria (Mound #21) genomes in the Mound Spring population.
source: In the Mound Spring population, we also identified key genes (dsrAB) responsible for dissimilatory sulfate reduction from Nitrospirae (Mound #19) and Termodesulfobacteria (Mound #21) genomes (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Mini-metagenomics uses occurrence of genomes across sub-samples to estimate abundance through counting cells.
source: Unlike typical shotgun metagenomic methods that use coverage depth as a proxy for genome abundance, mini-metagenomics uses occurrence of genomes across sub-samples to estimate abundance through counting cells.
evidence: This is a description of the method for abundance estimation.

claim: Thresholding coverage depth into an occurrence profile can be seen as digitizing an otherwise noisy analog signal, potentially reducing the effect of amplification bias, copy number variation, and genome size across genomes.
source: Thresholding coverage depth into an occurrence profile can be seen as digitizing an otherwise noisy analog signal, potentially reducing the effect of amplification bias, copy number variation, and genome size across genomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the methodological approach.

claim: Cells were distributed randomly into microfluidic chambers, with occurrence profiles satisfying a Poisson distribution.
source: Because cells were well-mixed before loading into the Fluidigm C1 IFC and that the microfluidic structures inside each chamber were much larger than the size of a microbial cell, cells were distributed randomly into microfluidic chambers, with occurrence profiles satisfying a Poisson distribution.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical distribution of cells, based on the experimental design.

claim: Assembled genomes from the Bijah sample covered one order of magnitude in abundance.
source: Assembled genomes from the Bijah sample covered one order of magnitude in abundance.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the abundance range observed in the Bijah sample.

claim: Genomes #10 (Deferribacteres) and #8 (Chlorobi) were most abundant in the Bijah sample, with 49 and 29 cells represented.
source: Genomes #10 (Deferribacteres) and #8 (Chlorobi) were most abundant, with 49 and 29 cells represented.
evidence: This claim is supported by abundance quantification data.

claim: Bijah #5 (S2R-29) was only represented in four sub-samples, most likely representing only four cells.
source: On the lower end, Bijah #5 (S2R-29) was only represented in four sub-samples, most likely representing only four cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by occurrence data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: In the Mound Spring sample, genomes covered two orders of magnitude in abundance.
source: In the Mound Spring sample, more sub-samples were sequenced, allowing the quantification of a larger abundance range across two orders of magnitude (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by abundance data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Mound #40 (Ignavibacteria) was the most abundant lineage, appearing in all but seven sub-samples.
source: Mound #40 (Ignavibacteria) was the most abundant lineage, appearing in all but seven sub-samples.
evidence: This is a direct report of abundance data.

claim: The abundance of Mound #40 genome was likely the reason for the successful assembly of its entire genome.
source: The abundance of this genome was likely the reason for the successful assembly of its entire genome (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between abundance and assembly success.

claim: Mound #11 (Bacteroidetes) and Mound #14 (Bathyarchaeota) were present at <1%.
source: For rare organisms, we detected Mound #11 (Bacteroidetes) and Mound #14 (Bathyarchaeota), which were present at <1%.
evidence: This is a direct report of abundance data for rare organisms.

claim: General agreement in relative abundance profiles was observed when comparing mini-metagenomic and shotgun coverage methods.
source: Comparing with relative abundance computed from shotgun coverage, we observed general agreement in relative abundance profiles, although a couple of genomes in Bijah Springs displayed large differences (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Relative abundances were higher for less abundant genomes when the mini-metagenomic method was used, demonstrating its sensitivity to extracting rare phylogenies.
source: Relative abundances were higher for less abundant genomes when the mini-metagenomic method was use, demonstrating its sensitivity to extracting rare phylogenies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Examining genomes larger than 0.5 Mbp, 192 and 509 cells were captured from Bijah and Mound Springs, respectively, corresponding to four to six cells per sub-sample.
source: In total, examining genomes larger than 0.5 Mbp, we captured 192 and 509 cells from Bijah and Mound Springs, respectively, corresponding to four to six cells per sub-sample.
evidence: This is a direct report of cell capture data.

claim: The difference between intended ten cells per chamber and observed four to six cells was likely due to lysis inefficiency or smaller genomes excluded from analysis.
source: Even though this number was smaller than our intended ten cells per chamber, the difference was likely due to lysis inefficiency or smaller genomes excluded from our analysis.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in cell numbers.

claim: All Ignavibacteriae and three Bacteroidetes genomes have low SNP rates (<1%).
source: All Ignavibacteriae and three Bacteroidetes genomes have low SNP rates (<1%).
evidence: This is a direct report of SNP analysis data.

claim: In the Bijah Spring sample, members of Spirochaetes, Microgenomates, and S2R-29 contain the most SNPs at 0.3–0.4% of the assembled genome.
source: In the Bijah Spring sample, members of Spirochaetes, Microgenomates, and S2R-29 contain the most SNPs at 0.3–0.4% of the assembled genome.
evidence: This is a direct report of SNP analysis data.

claim: In the Mound Spring sample, members of Thermodesulfobacteria have the most SNPs (0.6%).
source: In the Mound Spring sample, members of Thermodesulfobacteria have the most SNPs (0.6%).
evidence: This is a direct report of SNP analysis data.

claim: It is not the case that larger, more complete, or more abundant genomes contain more SNPs in a population.
source: It is not the case that larger, more complete, or more abundant genomes contain more SNPs in a population (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that the observed SNP rate is a biological property of the particular genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed SNP rate is a biological property of the particular genome.
source: It is not the case that larger, more complete, or more abundant genomes contain more SNPs in a population (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that the observed SNP rate is a biological property of the particular genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between genome properties and SNP rates.

claim: The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous SNP rates (dN/dS) is typically a measure of the strength of environmental selection.
source: The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous SNP rates (dN/dS) is typically a measure of the strength of environmental selection (Holt et al., 2008), with one indicating no selection and zero indicating strong selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Holt et al., 2008 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Among diverse genomes, dN/dS ranging from 0.4 to 0.9 was found in the hot spring genomes, illustrating that different phylogenies in the same hot spring environment are subjected to different weak to moderate negative selection pressures.
source: Among diverse genomes that allow more accurate assessment of SNP ratios, we found dN/dS ranging from 0.4 to 0.9 in the hot spring genomes, illustrating that different phylogenies in the same hot spring environment are subjected to different weak to moderate negative selection pressures.
evidence: This claim is supported by dN/dS analysis data.

claim: Previous work has implemented similar concepts of sequencing multiple bacterial cells together in order to increase throughput.
source: Previous work has implemented similar concepts of sequencing multiple bacterial cells together in order to increase throughput.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work in the field.

claim: Previous authors treated each sub-sample as an independent entity throughout their bioinformatic analysis.
source: However, the authors treated each sub-sample as an independent entity throughout their bioinformatic analysis (McLean et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McLean et al., 2013.

claim: The novelty of the analysis derives from treating information from sub-samples as different but overlapping sections of a more complex metagenome.
source: The novelty of our analysis derives from treating information from sub-samples as different but overlapping sections of a more complex metagenome.
evidence: This is a statement about the novel aspect of the method.

claim: Recent work uses coverage from many shotgun metagenomic samples containing a similar set of microbial phylogenies but with different abundances in order to aid bioinformatic genome binning.
source: Such an approach echoes recent work that uses coverage from many shotgun metagenomic samples containing a similar set of microbial phylogenies but with different abundances in order to aid bioinformatic genome binning (Alneberg et al., 2014; Nielsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alneberg et al., 2014 and Nielsen et al., 2014.

claim: The mini-metagenomic approach generates sub-samples from one, possibly low volume, microbial sample, eliminating the need to collect multiple spatial or temporal metagenomic samples.
source: First, our approach generates sub-samples from one, possibly low volume, microbial sample, eliminating the need to collect multiple spatial or temporal metagenomic samples.
